Mild discomfort that settles within a day or so is usually fine, but pain that is much worse the next day means you should do less.

content:
Walking is one of the simplest ways to stay active, and walking with others can add motivation and company. If you live with arthritis and frailty, a slow, short group walk may feel more manageable than walking alone.

This guide explains the benefits, how to find a group, and how to pace yourself. It is educational information, not personal medical advice.

Benefits

The NHS recommends that older adults do some activity every day, including activities to improve strength, balance and flexibility. NICE recommends exercise as a core treatment for osteoarthritis. Walking can help with stiffness, mood and confidence, and groups can reduce loneliness.

Finding a group

  • Walking for Health, run by the Ramblers in England, offers free short walks, some of them graded as easy or short.
  • Ask your GP practice about social prescribing, which can link you to local walks.
  • Local councils, leisure centres, libraries and charities may run gentle walks.

Getting started safely

  • Ask the leader about the length, terrain and pace before you go.
  • Use your usual walking aid and wear supportive shoes.
  • Start with a short walk and build up gradually.
  • Take water, and rest when you need to.
  • Tell the leader if you have a health condition that could affect you.

Is it too much?

Some discomfort during and after exercise is common with arthritis and is not usually harmful. If pain is much worse the next day, or lasts more than a day or two, do a shorter or easier walk next time. Stop if you feel dizzy, chest pain or very breathless, and seek advice.

Walking sports and other options

Walking football, walking netball and similar sports are slower versions of team games. They can be fun, but involve turning and stopping, which can be harder on painful joints and balance. Check with your physiotherapist and start slowly. Seated exercise or tai chi may be better if balance is poor.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

What if I can only walk a few minutes?

That is a good start. Some groups offer very short walks, or you can walk in short bursts with rests.

Should I use a stick on group walks?

Yes, if you usually use one. Tell the leader so they can choose suitable routes.

Can I join if I use a wheelchair or scooter?

Some groups have accessible routes. Ask the organiser.
